title: The quiet terminal experiment
paragraphs: For years, announcements at Westhaven Airport had repeated information already displayed on screens. Travelers complained about the noise, while staff argued that frequent announcements prevented passengers from missing flights. When the airport tested a quieter terminal, managers agreed to announce only urgent changes and final boarding calls. Routine information would remain on screens and in the airport app. The trial lasted six weeks, covering both busy and quiet periods.

At first, the results appeared straightforward. Noise complaints fell sharply, and surveys showed that most passengers preferred the calmer atmosphere. Yet the airport's accessibility team warned against treating the average score as the whole story. Some passengers could not comfortably read distant screens. Others had phones without an internet connection or found the app difficult to use. These groups were small in the survey, partly because the questionnaire itself was offered through the app.

Rather than abandon the trial, the airport installed additional screens at sitting height and introduced clearly marked assistance points. Staff also offered passengers a choice of receiving essential updates by text message. The number of missed flights did not increase during the second half of the trial, although managers admitted that six weeks was too short to judge every seasonal situation.

The final report recommended keeping the quieter policy with the new support measures. Its authors resisted describing the experiment as a simple victory for technology. The app had helped some travelers, but the improvement depended equally on physical signs and available staff. An airport could become quieter without becoming less informative, they concluded, provided that information reached passengers in more than one way.

questions.question: Which announcements continued during the trial?
options: No announcements at all
Urgent changes and final boarding calls
Every routine update
Only messages about the app
questions.evidence: announce only urgent changes and final boarding calls.
questions.explanation: Zmniejszono liczbę komunikatów, ale nie usunięto wszystkich.

questions.question: Why might the survey have understated accessibility problems?
options: The survey used a tool some affected passengers could not easily use
Only airport workers answered it
Noise complaints were deleted
Everyone had to answer in person
questions.evidence: the questionnaire itself was offered through the app.
questions.explanation: Forma ankiety mogła wykluczać część osób mających trudności z aplikacją.

questions.question: How did the airport respond to the warning?
options: It restored every announcement immediately
It stopped asking for feedback
It required every passenger to buy a phone
It added several ways to obtain information
questions.evidence: additional screens at sitting height and introduced clearly marked assistance points.
questions.explanation: Uzupełnił rozwiązanie o ekrany i pomoc personelu, zamiast polegać wyłącznie na telefonach.

questions.question: What limitation did managers acknowledge?
options: More people definitely missed flights
The new screens were too expensive
The trial did not cover every seasonal condition
The app never worked
questions.evidence: six weeks was too short to judge every seasonal situation.
questions.explanation: Wniosek ma ograniczony zakres czasowy; brak wzrostu spóźnień nie dowodzi skuteczności w każdej sytuacji.

questions.question: Which conclusion best represents the report?
options: Quiet terminals can have no spoken announcements
A calmer environment still needs accessible information through several channels
Technology should replace airport staff
Most passengers should decide what everyone needs
questions.evidence: provided that information reached passengers in more than one way.
questions.explanation: Warunkiem sukcesu jest różnorodny, dostępny przekaz informacji.

title: A label is only a beginning
paragraphs: A restaurant chain decided to mark dishes that could be prepared without certain common ingredients. The new menu used simple symbols, and managers expected ordering to become easier. During training, however, a chef pointed out that changing an ingredient was not the same as preventing all contact with it. A sauce could be left off a plate, for example, while the equipment used to prepare the meal might still have touched that sauce earlier.

The company revised the wording before printing the menus. Instead of making a broad promise, the symbols invited customers to discuss their needs with staff. Some managers worried that this extra conversation would slow service and make the labels seem less useful. The chef argued that a quick but misleading answer was worse than a slightly longer, accurate one. Staff were given a list of preparation procedures and told whom to consult when they were uncertain.

After three months, the chain reviewed customer comments and a sample of orders. Fewer meals had to be returned because of misunderstood requests. The review did not prove that every kitchen followed every procedure perfectly, and the company continued its inspections. It did suggest that the conversations were helping customers make informed choices.

The most useful feedback came from a customer who rarely ordered the same dish twice. She said the symbols helped her begin a conversation, not avoid one. What reassured her was a server who could explain the limits of the information and check with the kitchen. The chain kept the labels, but its next training session focused less on remembering symbols and more on asking clear questions and admitting uncertainty.

questions.question: What distinction did the chef make?
options: Changing ingredients differs from preventing contact during preparation
All sauces contain the same ingredients
Labels are always less accurate than memory
Customers never read menus
questions.evidence: changing an ingredient was not the same as preventing all contact with it.
questions.explanation: Skład gotowego dania i kontakt podczas przygotowania to odrębne kwestie.

questions.question: Why were the menu symbols reworded?
options: To hide ingredient information
To remove all special requests
To encourage customers to order faster
To avoid promising more than the kitchen could guarantee
questions.evidence: Instead of making a broad promise, the symbols invited customers to discuss their needs with staff.
questions.explanation: Symbole stały się początkiem rozmowy, a nie bezwarunkową gwarancją.

questions.question: What did the review establish?
options: Customers stopped asking questions
Inspections were no longer necessary
Misunderstood orders were returned less often
Every kitchen procedure was always followed
questions.evidence: Fewer meals had to be returned because of misunderstood requests.
questions.explanation: Wynik dotyczył zwrotów z powodu nieporozumień; tekst wyraźnie ogranicza szersze wnioski.

questions.question: What reassured the customer most?
options: Always ordering the same meal
A server who explained limits and checked details
The absence of symbols
A promise that every dish was suitable
questions.evidence: a server who could explain the limits of the information and check with the kitchen.
questions.explanation: Klientka ceniła rzetelność i weryfikację, a nie sam znak graficzny.

questions.question: What is the writer's main point?
options: Clear communication includes acknowledging what is not yet known
Detailed menus eliminate the need for staff training
Fast service should be avoided
Uncertainty makes all information useless
questions.evidence: asking clear questions and admitting uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Rzetelność obejmuje jasne pytania i uczciwe komunikowanie niepewności.

title: What the shorter week changed
paragraphs: A design company tested a four-day working week without reducing salaries. Before the trial, its director predicted that a longer weekend would make employees more productive. The staff were enthusiastic, but the team responsible for customer support was worried. Clients would still expect replies on Fridays, and simply closing the office could shift work into an unpaid day at home.

The company therefore arranged different days off for different teams. It also shortened regular meetings, stopped requiring two managers to approve small purchases, and introduced a shared record of decisions. These changes were meant to prevent the same work from being squeezed into fewer hours. Employees recorded both their official working time and any time spent checking messages outside it.

At the end of the trial, completed projects and customer satisfaction had remained stable. Staff reported feeling less tired, and after-hours messaging had fallen. The director initially described the result as proof that four days were enough for any office. An internal analyst objected. The trial had combined several changes, so it was impossible to know how much of the benefit came from the extra day off rather than the simpler procedures. The company also had a relatively predictable workload during those months.

They decided to keep the shorter week, but the public report used more careful language. It described what had worked in that company and listed the conditions that had helped. Another business might need a different schedule, the report noted. The director accepted the revision. A less dramatic claim would be less useful in an advertisement, but more useful to employers deciding whether to run their own trial.

questions.question: What concerned the support team?
options: Salaries would automatically fall
Clients wanted fewer replies
The company had no Friday clients
Work might continue unofficially on the day off
questions.evidence: shift work into an unpaid day at home.
questions.explanation: Obawiano się ukrytej pracy, a nie tylko zamkniętego biura.

questions.question: Why were procedures simplified?
options: To make employees work faster without breaks
To stop recording decisions
To reduce unnecessary work rather than compress it
To remove all managers
questions.evidence: prevent the same work from being squeezed into fewer hours.
questions.explanation: Zmieniono organizację, aby krótszy tydzień nie oznaczał jedynie większego ścisku.

questions.question: Why did the analyst challenge the director's claim?
options: The company had cut salaries
Several factors had changed at once
Every project was late
The staff disliked the trial
questions.evidence: The trial had combined several changes
questions.explanation: Nie da się przypisać całego efektu wyłącznie wolnemu dniowi, gdy zmieniono także procedury.

questions.question: What does stable customer satisfaction show?
options: Service quality did not obviously decline in this trial
Every company can close on Fridays
Customers knew nothing about the change
The shorter week increased sales
questions.evidence: customer satisfaction had remained stable.
questions.explanation: To ograniczony wynik badania, nie uniwersalny dowód ani informacja o sprzedaży.

questions.question: Why was the revised report useful?
options: It guaranteed identical results everywhere
It avoided mentioning limitations
It was written mainly as an advertisement
It described conditions others could compare with their own
questions.evidence: listed the conditions that had helped.
questions.explanation: Podanie warunków pomaga innym ocenić, czy rozwiązanie jest dla nich odpowiednie.

title: The cleanup that changed direction
paragraphs: Every spring, residents of Brookfield collected litter from the riverbank. The event was popular, and photos of full rubbish bags appeared in the local newspaper. After several years, volunteer organizer Mei began to question what those photos actually showed. A large collection could mean that the team had worked hard, but it could also mean that more waste was reaching the river. The same figure could tell two very different stories.

Mei asked volunteers to record the kinds of litter they found and the places where it collected. Many assumed visitors to the riverside park were responsible. The records showed plenty of food packaging, but a surprisingly large amount of material came from construction sites upstream. Heavy rain carried it through drains to the river. The park remained part of the problem, just not the whole problem.

The volunteers shared their observations with local builders and the council. Some builders objected that the records did not identify which site had produced each piece of waste. Mei agreed and avoided accusing individual companies. Instead, she proposed better covers for storage areas and regular checks of nearby drains. Several companies joined a small trial, while the annual cleanup continued.

The following spring, the volunteers collected fewer bags. Attendance was similar, and the same stretch of river had been covered. This was encouraging, but Mei cautioned that rainfall had also been lower. She wanted another year's records before making a strong claim about the trial. The newspaper still printed a photograph, this time of volunteers sorting a smaller pile. Its caption explained why less rubbish could represent more progress.

questions.question: Why did Mei question the original success measure?
options: Volunteers were no longer attending
Nobody counted the bags
More collected rubbish could also indicate a worsening problem
The photographs were fake
questions.evidence: The same figure could tell two very different stories.
questions.explanation: Wysoka liczba worków może oznaczać wysiłek albo narastające zanieczyszczenie.

questions.question: What did the records change?
options: The timing of every storm
The belief that park visitors explained the whole problem
The fact that any litter came from the park
The location of the river
questions.evidence: The park remained part of the problem, just not the whole problem.
questions.explanation: Nowe dane poszerzyły wyjaśnienie; nie wykluczyły odpowiedzialności odwiedzających park.

questions.question: Why did Mei avoid naming particular builders?
options: The evidence did not link individual waste to individual sites
She wanted to stop collecting data
All builders had refused to help
The council had banned criticism
questions.evidence: did not identify which site had produced each piece of waste.
questions.explanation: Zakres dowodów nie pozwalał przypisać każdego odpadu konkretnej firmie.

questions.question: Why was the smaller pile not conclusive proof?
options: The volunteers cleaned a different river
Nobody attended that year
The newspaper refused a photograph
Lower rainfall could also have affected the result
questions.evidence: rainfall had also been lower.
questions.explanation: Mniej deszczu to alternatywne wyjaśnienie mniejszej ilości naniesionych odpadów.

questions.question: What does the final caption emphasize?
options: Photographs are more useful than records
The cleanup should measure only attendance
A smaller visible output may indicate a better underlying result
More rubbish always means more progress
questions.evidence: less rubbish could represent more progress.
questions.explanation: Cel to czystsza rzeka, a nie maksymalna liczba pełnych worków.

title: Who came after dark?
paragraphs: A city museum extended its Friday opening hours to attract people who could not visit during the day. The first evening event included live music and free entry. More than twice the usual number of visitors arrived, and the museum announced that the new hours had been a success. Yet one curator wanted to know whether those visitors were the people the change was intended to reach.

A short survey showed that many already visited regularly. They enjoyed the music and had invited friends who also had flexible schedules. People working late shifts were still poorly represented. Several said that the last bus from the museum left before their work ended. Others had not heard about the event because the advertising had mainly reached the museum's existing mailing list.

For the next series, the museum worked with local employers and placed posters at transport stops. It arranged a modest bus service from two workplaces and offered short tours that visitors could join without booking. The total attendance was lower than at the music event. However, a much larger share of visitors said it was their first museum visit in several years. Staff also noticed that these visitors asked different questions about the displays, prompting plans for new labels.

The museum did not stop holding concerts. They were enjoyable and helped raise money. It simply began reporting the two kinds of event separately. Large crowds and broader access were both valuable, but they were not interchangeable measures. The curator's question had not disproved the first event's success; it had clarified what kind of success it actually represented and what still needed to change.

questions.question: What was the original purpose of longer opening hours?
options: To remove the need for transport
To reach people unable to visit during the day
To replace all daytime visits
To attract only regular visitors
questions.evidence: attract people who could not visit during the day.
questions.explanation: Cel dotyczył dostępności dla konkretnej grupy, nie samej frekwencji.

questions.question: Why did the first event not fully meet that purpose?
options: It mainly reached people already able to attend
The music was unpopular
The museum closed earlier
No advertising was used
questions.evidence: many already visited regularly.
questions.explanation: Duży tłum nie oznaczał automatycznie dotarcia do nowych, pomijanych odbiorców.

questions.question: Which practical barrier did the later series address?
options: The cost of every museum object
A lack of musicians
A ban on questions
Transport from workplaces
questions.evidence: arranged a modest bus service from two workplaces
questions.explanation: Organizatorzy dodali dojazd z miejsc pracy.

questions.question: Why could the smaller second audience be encouraging?
options: It spent more on concerts
It needed no additional support
It included more people who had not visited for years
It contained only staff
questions.evidence: a much larger share of visitors said it was their first museum visit in several years.
questions.explanation: Skład publiczności lepiej odpowiadał celowi zwiększenia dostępu.

questions.question: What does 'not interchangeable' mean here?
options: The museum must choose a single purpose forever
One measure cannot simply stand in for the other
Both measures are worthless
Only large crowds matter
questions.evidence: Large crowds and broader access were both valuable, but they were not interchangeable measures.
questions.explanation: Duża frekwencja i poszerzenie dostępu to różne, choć oba wartościowe wyniki.
